title: Incompressible Quantum Information
authors: Lasse H. Wolff, Matthias Christandl, Bergfinnur Durhuus, Christoph Hirche, Andreas Winter
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.
tldr: The paper shows that, unlike classical correlated systems, quantum systems can be incompressible: compressing a large quantum system while preserving correlations with a small reference system can destroy a significant amount of mutual information.
motivation: Classical information-bottleneck intuitions suggest that correlations with a small system allow efficient compression of a large correlated system; the authors test whether this remains true for quantum systems.
method: The authors construct bipartite quantum states and prove bounds showing that any nontrivial compression of the large subsystem necessarily reduces mutual information with the small subsystem by a significant amount.
result: They identify quantum states for which compression by any non-trivial relative factor destroys a non-negligible amount of correlation, measured by mutual information, in sharp contrast with the classical case.
conclusion: These results reveal a fundamental limitation of information-bottleneck approaches in quantum machine learning, since a compact feature representation does not guarantee preservation of relevant quantum correlations.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates the compressibility of correlations between a small quantum system and a large quantum system, contrasting with the classical case where the large system can always be compressed to a size dependent only on the small system while preserving correlations up to a controllable error. The authors show that this classical intuition fails dramatically in the quantum setting: there exist bipartite quantum states such that any non-trivial compression of the large system (i.e., reducing its dimension by a constant factor) necessarily destroys a significant amount of correlation, as quantified by mutual information. The result is proven by constructing explicit families of states and using information-theoretic arguments, including entropy inequalities and decoupling theorems. The paper identifies a fundamental limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, where a small system specifying relevant features of a large quantum dataset does not guarantee a compact encoding that preserves the relevant correlations. The work is theoretical, with 6 pages of main text and 17 pages of appendices, and no figures.

Provides explicit constructions of bipartite states that exhibit this strong incompressibility of correlations, demonstrating that the phenomenon is not an artifact of pathological cases but occurs in natural quantum states.

Quantifies the trade-off between compression factor and correlation loss, showing that the mutual information loss is bounded below by a constant when the compression factor is below a certain threshold.

title: Holevo-Bounded Total Information From Pair Distributions Of Alternative Quantum Measurements
authors: Baichu Yu, Zhang Zhou, Zhiyuan Li, Jiajun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The accessible information of a quantum ensemble can be strictly smaller than its Holevo information because a single-copy measurement may discard part of the label--system correlation. We ask whether information represented across two alternative measurement contexts can bridge this gap without assigning a joint distribution to their outcomes. Building on the relative-entropy-based projection method introduced by Harder et al., we define the directed posterior novelty of each record relative to the other, and an associated total-information quantity. For posterior-orthogonal records, this quantity equals the sum of the two record mutual informations. For finite-dimensional classical--quantum ensembles, we prove that optimizing this quantity over pairs of POVMs yields a value between the accessible and Holevo information. The upper bound follows by showing that the directed posterior novelty provides a lower bound on the infimum of the measured-relative-entropy recovery error. The uniform BB84 ensemble provides an example in which the quantity saturates the Holevo information while strictly exceeding the accessible information. Finally, we analytically establish the quantum validity of a redundancy-based information causality condition, resolving a question that has remained open since the condition was introduced.
tldr: The paper defines a Holevo-bounded total-information quantity from pairs of alternative POVMs and proves it interpolates between accessible and Holevo information for classical-quantum ensembles.
motivation: Accessible information can be strictly less than Holevo information because single-copy measurements discard label-system correlations; the authors ask whether information across two alternative measurement contexts can bridge this gap without a joint outcome distribution.
method: Building on a relative-entropy-based projection method, they define directed posterior novelty and an associated total-information quantity, then optimize over pairs of POVMs for finite-dimensional classical-quantum ensembles.
result: They prove the optimized quantity lies between accessible and Holevo information, show the uniform BB84 ensemble saturates Holevo while exceeding accessible information, and analytically establish quantum validity of a redundancy-based information-causality condition.
conclusion: The work provides an information-theoretic framework connecting alternative measurement contexts to Holevo and accessible information, with implications for quantum information measures and information causality.

The authors build on the relative-entropy-based projection method of Harder et al. to define a directed posterior novelty between two measurement records and an associated total-information quantity. For posterior-orthogonal records, this quantity reduces to the sum of the two record mutual informations. For finite-dimensional classical–quantum ensembles, they prove that optimizing this quantity over pairs of POVMs yields a value between the accessible and Holevo information. The upper bound is established by showing that the directed posterior novelty provides a lower bound on the infimum of the measured-relative-entropy recovery error. They illustrate with the uniform BB84 ensemble, where the quantity saturates the Holevo information while strictly exceeding the accessible information. Finally, they analytically prove the quantum validity of a redundancy-based information causality condition, resolving a question open since its introduction.

Proof that for finite-dimensional classical–quantum ensembles, optimizing this quantity over POVM pairs yields a value bounded between the accessible information and the Holevo information.

title: Time-Reversed Task Events And Thermodynamic Bounds For Stochastic Thermal Machines
authors: Kaiyuan Cao, Bei Xiao, Jian Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a task-based framework that relates finite-time performance to thermodynamic irreversibility in stochastic heat engines and refrigerators. For tasks defined by reaching an accumulated-work threshold within a prescribed time, we construct the reverse event through exact trajectory time reversal. The binary relative entropy between forward and reverse task probabilities provides a lower bound on mean entropy production. Combined with the first law and entropy balance, this bound constrains irreversible work loss in engines and excess input work in refrigerators. We illustrate the framework with a three-level stochastic system and test the bounds against its full dynamics. These results show how success-or-failure statistics alone can reveal irreversibility and constrain the energetic costs of finite-time thermal tasks. We also outline an experimental route to testing the framework using a monitored three-level system coupled to engineered thermal reservoirs and a work channel.
tldr: The paper develops a task-based framework linking finite-time success probabilities of stochastic heat engines and refrigerators to thermodynamic irreversibility via exact trajectory time reversal.
motivation: Finite-time thermal machines incur irreversible losses, and there is a need for bounds that connect observable task success-or-failure statistics to entropy production and energetic costs.
method: For tasks defined by reaching an accumulated-work threshold within a fixed time, the authors construct reverse events through exact trajectory time reversal and derive a binary relative-entropy lower bound on mean entropy production, combined with the first law and entropy balance.
result: The bound constrains irreversible work loss in engines and excess input work in refrigerators, and is illustrated and tested against the full dynamics of a three-level stochastic system.
conclusion: Success-or-failure statistics alone can reveal irreversibility and constrain finite-time thermodynamic costs, with an outlined experimental route using a monitored three-level system coupled to engineered reservoirs and a work channel.

title: Distant Bell States Via Measured Spin Chain Dynamics
authors: Sougato Bose Ralph Jason Costales
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing distant qubits in Bell states is a core requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum computation. The nonequilibrium unitary dynamics of spin chains have been envisaged as a convenient quantum channel for intra-chip communications. Typically it establishes mixed entangled states between its remote ends, to be purified by entanglement distillation after several uses of the channel to obtain Bell states. Here we show how the establishment of entanglement via spin chain dynamics can be (a) sped up and (b) made to yield a pure entangled state after a single usage of the channel, which is upgradable to a Bell-state without the complexity of purification. To this end, we intersperse unitary evolution for some period with measurements on intermediary spins. We explore two different measurements: a measurement that post-selects for a ground state; and local measurements in the computational basis. We illustrate the mechanism with qubits coupled to the ends of a 1D [MATH] spin chain.
tldr: A scheme to generate distant Bell states via measured spin chain dynamics, enabling pure entangled states in a single channel use without purification.
motivation: Preparing distant Bell states is crucial for quantum networking and distributed quantum computation, but spin chain dynamics typically yield mixed states requiring distillation.
method: Intersperse unitary evolution of a 1D spin chain with measurements on intermediary spins, using either post-selection for ground state or local computational basis measurements.
result: The approach speeds up entanglement establishment and yields a pure entangled state after a single use, upgradable to a Bell state without purification.
conclusion: Measurement-assisted spin chain dynamics provide an efficient route to distant Bell states for quantum networking applications.

Typically, such dynamics generate mixed entangled states that require entanglement distillation over multiple channel uses to obtain pure Bell states. The authors propose to intersperse the unitary evolution with measurements on intermediary spins to achieve two goals: (a) speed up entanglement establishment and (b) obtain a pure entangled state after a single use of the channel, which can be upgraded to a Bell state without distillation. Two measurement strategies are explored: post-selecting on a ground state of an intermediary spin, and local measurements in the computational basis. The mechanism is illustrated with qubits coupled to the ends of the chain, and the authors analyze the resulting entanglement fidelity and success probability.

Two measurement types are considered: (1) a projective measurement that post-selects the intermediary spin in its ground state, and (2) local measurements in the computational basis (Z-basis) on one or more intermediary spins. The measurement outcomes are used to herald or post-select states, and the resulting state of the end qubits is analyzed for entanglement purity and fidelity to a Bell state. The approach leverages the measurement-induced non-unitary dynamics to effectively 'steer' the system into a pure entangled state, avoiding the need for repeated channel uses and distillation. title: Sharp Purity Based Entropy Bounds And Machine Learning Assisted Entropy Estimation
authors: Shree Prakash Komal Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness, motivating the study of its role in controlling entropy variations. A sharp purity-based continuity bound is established for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states. The bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound. In higher dimensions, an explicit sharp bound is derived within the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state. Further continuity estimates are obtained for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families. An application to machine learning assisted qubit entropy estimation illustrates how the sharp bound converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.
tldr: The paper establishes sharp purity-based continuity bounds for von Neumann entropy and related information measures, with an application to machine-learning-assisted qubit entropy estimation.
motivation: Purity controls mixedness and entropy variation, but existing purity-based entropy bounds are not tight; sharper continuity estimates would improve rigorous entropy certification and entanglement quantification.
method: The authors derive attainable continuity bounds for qubit von Neumann entropy as a function of purity difference, extend an explicit sharp bound to higher-dimensional states of the form pure plus maximally mixed, and obtain continuity estimates for conditional entropy, mutual information, conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement in restricted bipartite and tripartite families.
result: The qubit bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound; the higher-dimensional bound is sharp within the specified family, and the ML application converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.
conclusion: These results provide sharper information-theoretic continuity tools and demonstrate how purity estimation can rigorously certify entropy in learning-assisted settings.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper establishes sharp continuity bounds on von Neumann entropy and related information measures in terms of purity (or its square). For qubit states, it proves a tight inequality relating the entropy difference to the purity difference, which is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves upon the existing purity-based bound. The bound is derived by analyzing the geometry of the Bloch sphere and the binary entropy function, leading to a closed-form expression that is optimal. In higher dimensions, the authors derive an explicit sharp bound within the family of states formed by mixing a pure state with the maximally mixed state, showing that the bound is tight for that family. They then extend the continuity estimates to conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement for specified bipartite and tripartite families, using the qubit bound as a building block. Finally, they illustrate an application to machine learning-assisted qubit entropy estimation, where the sharp bound rigorously converts purity estimation errors into entropy error bounds, enabling certified entropy estimation from purity measurements.

An explicit sharp bound in higher dimensions for the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state.
Continuity estimates for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is primarily analytical, leveraging the Bloch sphere representation for qubits and the properties of the binary entropy function. The authors formulate the problem as an optimization: for a given purity difference, find the maximum possible entropy difference. By exploiting the concavity of entropy and the geometry of the state space, they derive a closed-form expression for the sharp bound. The proof likely involves showing that the extremal states are those with Bloch vectors aligned along a certain direction, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional optimization. For higher dimensions, they restrict to the family of states that are convex combinations of a pure state and the maximally mixed state, where the entropy depends only on the mixing parameter, and derive a tight bound within that family. The extension to composite systems uses chain rules and the qubit bound to bound conditional entropies and mutual informations, with careful accounting of the purities of subsystems. The machine learning application uses standard estimation techniques, and the bound provides a rigorous error propagation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the qubit bound: for two qubit states with purities P and Q (where P = Tr(ρ^2)), the entropy difference is bounded by a function of |P - Q| that is tight for all possible purity differences. Specifically, the bound is expressed in terms of the binary entropy and the purity, and it strictly improves upon the previously known bound by a factor that depends on the purity. The attainability is shown by constructing states that saturate the inequality. In higher dimensions, for states of the form ρ = p|ψ⟩⟨ψ| + (1-p)I/d, the entropy is a function of p, and the bound is sharp within this family. The extensions to conditional entropy and mutual information yield bounds that are tight for certain families, such as when the conditioning subsystem is a qubit. The squashed entanglement bound is derived for tripartite states with a qubit subsystem. The machine learning application demonstrates that purity estimation errors of order ε lead to entropy error bounds of order ε^{1/2} near pure states, which is tighter than previous bounds.

title: Phase-dependent Atomicity And Ppt Edge States For Cyclic-sign Covariant Qutrit Maps
authors: Adam Rutkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decomposable positive maps cannot detect entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT). title: Causal Consistency And Cost Of Quantum Control
authors: Jeongho Bang, Kyoungho Cho, Jeongwoo Jae
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An unknown quantum state can supply the information needed to control a computation, but how much quantum data must be consumed to perform a prescribed action? We connect this resource question to causal consistency within the quantum state space. No-signaling requires identical observable predictions for remotely chosen ensemble preparations of the same complete input; quantum distinguishability then converts this requirement into finite-copy bounds. For amplitude amplification, we identify an exact low-copy obstruction and establish a dimension-independent, optimal quadratic dependence of the copy cost on angular gain at fixed accuracy, uniformly over arbitrary pure inputs. A coherent protocol attains this scaling without reconstructing a classical state description. Prior knowledge of a real two-level family additionally permits exponentially decreasing error with the copy budget at fixed gain. These results separate the resources needed to perform a specified quantum operation from those needed for universal state reconstruction. The central connection is operational: physical consistency restricts which distinctions a controller can expose, and the information carried by its complete input determines the cost of doing so. This links a causal requirement to quantitative limits on converting quantum data into computational control.
tldr: The paper relates causal consistency and no-signaling to quantitative copy-cost limits for using an unknown quantum state to control a computation, with sharp results for amplitude amplification.
motivation: It asks how much quantum data must be consumed to perform a prescribed action, separating the resources for a specific quantum operation from those needed for full state reconstruction.
method: The authors use no-signaling and quantum distinguishability to derive finite-copy bounds, then analyze amplitude amplification to identify low-copy obstructions and optimal scaling of copy cost with angular gain.
result: They establish a dimension-independent optimal quadratic copy-cost scaling with angular gain at fixed accuracy for arbitrary pure inputs, attained by a coherent protocol without classical state reconstruction, and show exponentially decreasing error under prior knowledge of a real two-level family.
conclusion: The work links causal consistency to operational limits on converting quantum data into computational control and clarifies resource separation between targeted quantum operations and universal state reconstruction.

title: Foliated Surface Codes For Optimal Skip-gate Leakage Correction
authors: Runjiang Bi, Nikita Astrakhantsev, Thomas B. Smith, Margaret Pavlovich, Ming Li, Shruti Puri
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skip-gate leakage --- such as atom loss in neutral-atom arrays or trapped ions, or photon loss in superconducting dual-rail qubits --- takes a qubit out of its computational subspace and removes subsequent gates acting on it. If leakage is only detectable end-of-the-line at qubit measurement, error correction circuits must be designed to periodically measure all qubits, as in SWAP-based circuits and foliation. We show that the best SWAP-based surface code, although optimal against space-like skip-gate leakage errors, is suboptimal against time-like leakage errors. By optimal, we mean that the code corrects as many leakage errors as it can detect. Remarkably, we find that the foliated surface code is optimal against both space- and time-like error configurations. We support our findings with numerical simulations. Under two-qubit gate leakage with probability 0.5%, foliation suppresses time-like errors in a distance-4 rotated stability experiment by 1380(50) per two added rounds, compared to 63(1) for the best SWAP-based circuit. In memory, the two are comparable. Under an experimentally motivated neutral-atom noise model, we find that foliation outperforms SWAP-based circuits in stability for both rotated and unrotated code geometries. This holds true for a parameter sweep that takes the neutral-atom noise model from being dominated by computational errors to atom loss. Interestingly, a SWAP-based circuit for unrotated code memory performs best when computational noise dominates over loss. Our work motivates co-designing error correction circuits with logical operations: preferring foliation when time-like errors dominate and SWAP-based circuits when space-like errors dominate.

motivation: Skip-gate leakage, such as atom or photon loss, removes qubits from the computational subspace and disables subsequent gates, requiring error-correction circuits that periodically measure all qubits. Existing SWAP-based surface codes are optimal for space-like leakage but suboptimal for time-like leakage.
method: The authors analyze space-like and time-like skip-gate leakage configurations in SWAP-based and foliated surface codes, define optimality as correcting as many detectable leakage errors as possible, and support the analysis with numerical simulations under circuit-level and neutral-atom noise models.
result: Foliation is optimal against both space- and time-like errors, while the best SWAP-based circuit is only optimal against space-like errors. Under 0.5% two-qubit gate leakage, foliation suppresses time-like errors by 1380(50) per two added rounds in a distance-4 rotated stability experiment, compared to 63(1) for SWAP-based circuits.
conclusion: The work motivates co-designing error-correction circuits with logical operations, preferring foliation when time-like leakage dominates and SWAP-based circuits when space-like leakage dominates.

title: Tailored Magic States For Algorithmic Primitives
authors: Matthew Steinberg, Joseph Sullivan, Chunjun Cao, Michael Perlin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algorithmic primitives such as adders, multipliers, and Boolean logic typically contain clusters of multi-qubit non-Clifford gates, whose decomposition into [MATH] and [MATH] gates adds scheduling and spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Synthillation addresses this difficulty for diagonal circuits at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy by jointly synthesizing and distilling their non-Clifford content. In this work, we develop a complementary, code-theoretic approach to synthillation. We introduce CSS-T-Product (CSS-TP) codes, whose transversal single-qubit phase gates implement multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and give analytical rules that predict these logical gates from tensor-network operations. Using quantum LEGO, we generate code families with logical actions at the third and fourth levels of the Clifford hierarchy. We classify the resulting resource states as canonical (such as [MATH] or [MATH]), tensor products of canonical states, or irreducible, i.e., not reducible to a product of non-Clifford gates via Clifford operations and logical basis changes. Conversion into Encode-[MATH]-Decode factories built from these codes recover known synthillation resources and prepare magic states at higher levels of the Clifford hierarchy; we analyze them with a surface-code-based model for several algorithmic primitives. We demonstrate that tailored magic factories give significant latency improvements at similar or smaller occupied spacetime volume: at code distance [MATH] with one factory per resource family, they reduce the latency of a [MATH] multiplier and a shared-addend carry-lookahead adder by up to [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, and the smallest tailored factory also lowers the occupied spacetime volume. CSS-TP codes thus connect code construction to resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives.

motivation: Multi-qubit non-Clifford gates in adders and multipliers incur substantial scheduling and spacetime overhead when decomposed into T and Toffoli gates, motivating more efficient magic-state resource factories.
method: The authors define CSS-TP codes whose transversal single-qubit phase gates realize multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, derive tensor-network rules predicting these logical actions, and use quantum LEGO to generate code families at the third and fourth Clifford-hierarchy levels.

conclusion: CSS-TP codes connect code construction directly to resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives, enabling tailored magic-state production with improved fault-tolerant overhead.

title: Quantum Nonclassicality As A Marginal Problem
authors: Karl Svozil
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical explanations of quantum statistics---local, noncontextual, or causal---fail for one and the same reason: the probability distributions observed in different contexts are not the marginals of a single joint distribution. Every single context admits a classical model. This is Boole's problem of the "conditions of possible experience." Garg and Mermin treated it as a linear problem and showed, via Farkas's lemma, that its solvability is equivalent to a finite list of Bell-type inequalities, one for each extreme ray of a convex polyhedral cone; Pitowsky gave it the form of correlation polytopes. We sketch this common structure and discuss two examples: Aerts's elastic-band model, which reproduces the quantum cosine in one context but obeys the classical bound when contexts are combined; and nonclassicality in causal data fusion, where the contexts are supplied by interventions on a causal structure.
tldr: The paper sketches a unified marginal-problem perspective on quantum nonclassicality, linking Bell/noncontextual/causal inequalities to the nonexistence of a joint probability distribution.
motivation: Classical explanations of quantum statistics fail because context-dependent distributions are not marginals of one joint distribution; the author aims to present this common structural reason across different notions of nonclassicality.
method: The paper reviews the Boole–Garg–Mermin–Pitowsky formulation of contextuality and Bell inequalities via Farkas's lemma and correlation polytopes, then illustrates it with Aerts's elastic-band model and causal data fusion under interventions.
result: It shows that each individual context can admit a classical model while the combined contexts cannot, and that nonclassicality in causal data fusion fits the same marginal-problem template.
conclusion: Quantum nonclassicality can be understood uniformly as the failure of observed context-wise distributions to arise as marginals of a single joint distribution.

The paper emphasizes that each individual context admits a classical model; it is only the combination of contexts that reveals nonclassicality. Two illustrative examples are discussed: Aerts's elastic-band model, which reproduces the quantum cosine correlation in a single context but obeys the classical bound when contexts are combined, and nonclassicality in causal data fusion, where contexts arise from interventions on a causal structure. The paper is largely expository and synthetic, aiming to highlight the common mathematical structure underlying various no-go theorems rather than to present new technical results.

title: State-selective Dynamical Freezing In Driven Rydberg Atom Chains
authors: Madhumita Sarkar, Sougato Bose, Roopayan Ghosh
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical freezing, the near-complete suppression of dynamics at special drive frequencies, offers a route to mitigating Floquet heating in periodically driven quantum systems. In interacting systems, however, the energy cost of each transition depends on the many-body configuration, so that the freezing condition itself becomes state dependent. We study this dependence in periodically driven Rydberg atom chains under single- and bi-frequency driving. Using Floquet perturbation theory, we show that each spin flip is characterised by a single interference amplitude set by its local interaction shift, and that a state freezes only where the amplitudes of all its available flips vanish simultaneously. This picture accounts quantitatively for the shift and proliferation of freezing frequencies with interatomic spacing and for the response of entire families of initial states, which are sorted by a single local motif. Freezing is strong only within a window of spacings bounded by interaction tails on one side and nearest-neighbour excitation facilitation on the other, outside of which the advantage of bi-frequency driving is lost. In the regime of large detuning amplitude, where freezing points are numerous and the perturbative description is controlled, this window leaves almost no room for the PXP limit.
tldr: The paper analyzes state-selective dynamical freezing in periodically driven Rydberg atom chains, showing that freezing occurs only when interference amplitudes for all available spin flips vanish simultaneously.
motivation: Dynamical freezing can suppress Floquet heating, but in interacting systems the freezing condition becomes state dependent, motivating a quantitative understanding of this dependence.
method: The authors use Floquet perturbation theory to describe single- and bi-frequency driving of Rydberg chains, characterizing each spin flip by a local interference amplitude set by interaction shifts.
result: They find that freezing frequencies shift and proliferate with interatomic spacing, entire families of initial states are sorted by a local motif, and strong freezing exists only in a spacing window bounded by interaction tails and nearest-neighbour facilitation.
conclusion: State-selective freezing provides a quantitative picture of driven Rydberg chain dynamics and clarifies when bi-frequency driving can mitigate Floquet heating, with implications for the PXP limit.

title: Many-Body Flux Selection In Chiral Quantum Batteries
authors: Borhan Ahmadi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an interacting quantum-battery chain in which a synthetic flux controls interference between hopping paths. Keeping the internal battery Hamiltonian fixed, we seek the flux that leaves the most extractable work. Even a Gaussian reconstruction supplied with exact one-body information can rank competing flux settings incorrectly. A reduced many-body model that retains correlations within a few battery-occupation sectors recovers the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes across the finite systems and parameter ranges studied. Strikingly, the model can make an accurate control choice even when it excludes configurations carrying substantial probability in the exact state. Thus, choosing a nearly optimal charging flux can require much less information than reconstructing the full many-body state.

method: The author considers an interacting quantum-battery chain with a synthetic flux controlling hopping interference, compares exact many-body rankings of extractable work against a Gaussian reconstruction using one-body information, and introduces a reduced many-body model retaining correlations in selected battery-occupation sectors.
result: Gaussian reconstruction can misrank flux settings, while the reduced many-body model recovers the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes across the studied finite systems and parameter ranges, even when it excludes some high-probability configurations.
conclusion: Choosing a nearly optimal charging flux can require much less information than reconstructing the full many-body state, highlighting the role of targeted many-body correlations in quantum-battery control.

title: Long-time Dynamics Of Open Quantum Systems: Mathematical And Physical Aspects
authors: Daniele Amato, Paolo Facchi, Giovanni Gramegna, Arturo Konderak
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum channels provide the mathematical framework for describing the evolution of open quantum systems, i.e., quantum systems interacting with an environment. This review focuses on the long-time or asymptotic dynamics of open quantum systems, a topic of growing interest due to its relevance for quantum information theory and noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. We present a comprehensive analysis of homogeneous evolutions in both discrete and continuous time, treating the dynamics in full generality within the Schr\"odinger and Heisenberg pictures. By systematically studying the spectral properties of quantum channels, we present general structure theorems that characterize asymptotic behaviour, illustrated through several paradigmatic examples. We further discuss how the asymptotic dynamics can be exploited for dissipative state engineering, the identification of decoherence-free subspaces, the design of quantum error-correction schemes, and the evaluation of the asymptotic capacities of quantum channels.
tldr: A comprehensive review of the long-time asymptotic dynamics of open quantum systems described by quantum channels, with applications to decoherence-free subspaces, error correction, and asymptotic channel capacities.
motivation: Understanding asymptotic evolution of open quantum systems is increasingly important for quantum information theory and NISQ devices, where noise and dissipation dominate long-time behavior.
method: The authors systematically analyze spectral properties of quantum channels in discrete and continuous time, in both Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures, and derive general structure theorems for asymptotic dynamics.
result: The review characterizes asymptotic behavior through spectral channel theory and illustrates it with paradigmatic examples, discussing uses for dissipative state engineering, decoherence-free subspace identification, quantum error-correction design, and asymptotic channel capacities.
conclusion: The paper provides a unified mathematical and physical framework for long-time open-system dynamics, highlighting quantum-channel spectral methods as tools for quantum information applications.

title: Online Scheduling For Entanglement Distillation: Learning When To Wait
authors: Panagiotis Promponas, Spyros Tserkis, Leandros Tassiulas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.
tldr: A reinforcement learning policy for online scheduling of entanglement distillation operations that decides when to wait for outcomes to maximize throughput under decoherence.
motivation: Entanglement distillation is probabilistic and outcomes take time to communicate, causing decoherence; deciding whether to wait or proceed optimistically is a key challenge.
method: Formulates the problem as a Markov decision process and trains a policy using reinforcement learning; derives an upper bound on throughput.
result: Learned policy matches the better of always-wait or never-wait baselines when one is optimal, and outperforms otherwise.
conclusion: Online scheduling with learned policies can improve entanglement distillation throughput in quantum networks.

The key challenge is that each distillation operation's success or failure is only known after a communication delay, during which idle pairs decohere. The authors formulate the scheduling problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) and derive an upper bound on the achievable throughput of fidelity-constrained pairs for any policy. They then use reinforcement learning to train a policy that dynamically constructs distillation trees and decides, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome or proceed optimistically. The policy is designed to generalize across any number of quantum memories. Through simulations, they compare the learned policy against two baselines: one that always waits for outcomes and one that never waits. The results show that the learned policy matches the better baseline when one of these extremes is optimal and outperforms both otherwise, demonstrating the benefit of adaptive scheduling.

title: Increasing Quantum Ldpc Code Distance Through Explicit Extensions
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an explicit construction of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes without searching for candidates at each size. A fixed pair partition (PP) and fixed integer parameters determine the parity-check matrices at a specified size. Using affine permutation matrices (APMs), we construct a [MATH] code with column weight 3 and check weight 8 in each of the X and Z parity-check matrices. A construction based on circulant permutation matrices (CPMs) gives [MATH], with column weight 4 and check weight 10. We prove that the construction yields commuting checks and verify the resulting distances using exhaustive search and logical operators. For the main construction, we conjecture the existence of a finite structural distance upper bound and distance improvement toward that bound as the size increases.
tldr: The paper presents explicit, size-parameterized constructions of quantum LDPC codes with fixed column and check weights, based on affine and circulant permutation matrices, and analyzes their achievable distances.
motivation: Quantum LDPC codes are promising for low-overhead fault tolerance, but finding good codes typically requires exhaustive search at each block size; an explicit algebraic construction with predictable parameters would remove that search cost.
method: Using a fixed pair partition (PP) plus fixed integer parameters, the authors build X and Z parity-check matrices from affine permutation matrices (column weight 3, check weight 8) and, alternatively, circulant permutation matrices (column weight 4, check weight 10); they prove the checks commute and estimate distances via exhaustive search and logical-operator analysis.
result: The constructions yield commuting parity checks and verified code distances at the tested sizes, with the main family conjectured to obey a finite structural distance upper bound toward which the distance improves as the block length grows.
conclusion: The work gives a search-free route to qLDPC codes with controlled sparsity and empirically growing distance, though the asymptotic distance behavior remains a conjecture rather than a theorem.

title: Mitigating Large Circuits With A Learned Small-circuit Mitigator
authors: Thi Ha Kyaw, Pablo D\'iez-Valle, Gaurav Saxena
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90\% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.
tldr: The paper combines circuit cutting with a learned small-circuit error mitigator to extend learned quantum error mitigation to larger circuits without retraining per circuit.
motivation: Learned error mitigation is limited by the cost of exact training labels for large circuits and by poor generalization to larger or deeper circuits than those seen in training.
method: A small-circuit learned mitigator is trained once and reused on larger circuits by partitioning them via circuit cutting; the approach is benchmarked against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated random-circuit chains and a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver.
result: On random-circuit chains the fragment-wise mitigator removes most reconstructed error, and for the Ising-chain eigensolver it recovers close to 90% or more of the noise-induced energy error under a fixed shot budget, outperforming Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation.
conclusion: Circuit cutting enables practical reuse of learned error mitigators beyond the circuit sizes for which exact training labels are feasible, offering a modular and up-front-cost route to learned mitigation on larger quantum computations.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid approach that combines circuit cutting with learned quantum error mitigation to enable accurate inference on circuits larger and deeper than those used for training. The core idea is to train a machine-learning mitigator on small circuit fragments for which exact training labels (noise-free expectation values) can be efficiently computed via classical simulation, and then at inference time, cut a large target circuit into fragments that match the training distribution, apply the mitigator to each fragment, and reconstruct the full expectation value. This circumvents the exponential cost of exact training labels for large circuits and addresses the generalization challenge of learned mitigators to out-of-distribution circuit sizes and depths. The authors benchmark their fragment-wise mitigator against zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), Clifford data regression (CDR), and probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) on simulated random-circuit chains and a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver. For random-circuit chains, the method removes most of the reconstructed error. For the eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers close to 90% or more of the noise-induced energy error, outperforming CDR and PEC. The approach is modular: improvements to the small-circuit mitigator (e.g., retraining on larger fragments or device-specific noise) directly benefit all circuits that can be partitioned into such fragments. The cost is paid upfront during training rather than per circuit at inference, and no additional circuits or noise amplification are needed at inference time. The authors argue this offers a practical route to bring learned error mitigation to quantum computations beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided the circuits can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.

Provides a practical pathway to extend learned error mitigation to quantum computations that are otherwise intractable for exact training label generation, by leveraging circuit cutting with a moderate number of cuts.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology hinges on circuit cutting: a large circuit is partitioned into smaller fragments (subcircuits) that can be executed and mitigated individually. The authors train a machine-learning model (the 'fragment-wise mitigator') on small circuits for which exact noise-free expectation values are classically computable, using noisy measurement data as input. At inference, the target large circuit is cut into fragments that are statistically similar to the training fragments, the mitigator is applied to each fragment's noisy results, and the full expectation value is reconstructed via classical post-processing that accounts for the cutting (e.g., using quasi-probability decomposition or state reconstruction). The approach is compared against standard error mitigation techniques: ZNE, CDR, and PEC. The benchmarks use simulated circuits, including random-circuit chains and a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver, with circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. The training is done once, and inference requires no additional circuits or noise amplification, making the cost front-loaded. The modularity allows retraining on larger fragments or device-specific noise to improve all downstream circuits that can be cut into such fragments.

title: Quantum Metrology With Quantum Limit Cycles
authors: Zhi-Hao Liu, Xiangyu Niu, Keren Li, Ran Liu, Xiao-Dong Yang, Jun Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beyond nonclassical states, emergent quantum phenomena offer new metrological resources. Quantum limit cycles, in particular, sustain long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation. However, quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving their metrological performance unclear. Here, we propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by introducing nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol. We develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory to characterize its metrological performance, in good agreement with numerical simulations. The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size. We further combine limit-cycle dynamics with spin squeezing, finding that squeezing improves short-time precision, but phase diffusion ultimately dominates, leaving the asymptotic scaling unchanged. Our results establish quantum limit cycles as a metrological resource and clarify the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing.
tldr: The authors propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins that achieves Heisenberg-like scaling and analyze how spin squeezing and phase diffusion compete.
motivation: Emergent dynamical phenomena such as quantum limit cycles sustain long-lived coherent oscillations that could serve as metrological resources, but the impact of quantum fluctuations on their precision advantage was previously unclear.
method: Nonlinear damping is added to a conventional collective-decay protocol for collective spins, and a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory is developed and benchmarked against numerical simulations, including a combination with spin squeezing.
result: The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size; squeezing enhances short-time precision but phase diffusion dominates asymptotically, leaving the scaling exponent unchanged.
conclusion: Quantum limit cycles are established as a viable metrological resource, and the analysis clarifies the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing.

title: The Resource--invariant Gap: A Protected Floquet Invariant Need Not Protect Wigner Negativity
authors: Juste Deuyekbe, Philippe Djorw\'e, Nsangou Mama, S. G. Nana Engo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological invariants constrain a driven Floquet generator, yet whether they protect a transient nonlinear bosonic resource remains open. We track boundary Wigner negativity of an even cat state in a chiral Floquet Su--Schrieffer--Heeger chain with boundary Kerr nonlinearity and structured loss. The quasienergy windings remain quantized at every chain length, yet the matched sector contrast flips sign when the chain grows under index-end shielding and is null within [MATH] under uniform loss at [MATH] for [MATH]. Prepared and shielded on the physical dangling end, the contrast remains positive, modulated by local dimer return rather than set by the invariant. A three-site causal light cone and a boundary-Laplacian erosion law trace the flip to strong-bond bulk exposure: the sign is set by where the bulk-rate loss sits relative to the prepared site, not by chain length. We call this decoupling the resource--invariant gap.
tldr: The paper shows that a quantized Floquet topological invariant does not necessarily protect boundary Wigner negativity of a cat state in an open nonlinear SSH chain.
motivation: Topological invariants are often expected to protect quantum resources, but whether Floquet invariants protect transient bosonic nonclassicality in driven-dissipative systems is unclear.
method: The authors track Wigner negativity of an even cat state at the boundary of a chiral Floquet Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with boundary Kerr nonlinearity and structured loss, analyzing quasienergy windings and loss-induced sign changes.
result: Although quasienergy windings remain quantized, the matched-sector Wigner-negativity contrast can flip sign or vanish depending on where bulk-rate loss sits relative to the prepared site, rather than on chain length or the invariant.
conclusion: The findings reveal a resource-invariant gap: topological protection of a Floquet invariant need not extend to nonlinear bosonic resources such as Wigner negativity.

title: Photon Number Correlations In Harmonics Driven With Classical And Quantum Light
authors: Katarzyna M. Kowalczyk, Michael T. Weil, Kevin Murzyn, Andr\'e Staudte, Jeff S. Lundeen, David M. Villeneuve, Giulio Vampa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent reports of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised questions about whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily imply genuinely quantum behaviour. Here, we compare the low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical and bright squeezed vacuum sources. The latter generates strong auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and heralding measurements show that the cross-correlations are fully classical and can be explained by the common fluctuations from the driving field. A visible scaling of the measured correlation function with mean harmonic flux is observed, which is well-explained by a click detector-response model.
tldr: The paper shows that strong auto- and cross-correlations in perturbative harmonic generation driven by bright squeezed vacuum are fully classical and attributable to common driving-field fluctuations.
motivation: Recent observations of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised the question of whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily indicate genuinely quantum behavior.
method: The authors compare low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical light and bright squeezed vacuum, using Cauchy-Schwarz inequality tests and heralding measurements to distinguish quantum from classical correlations.
result: The cross-correlations violate neither classicality criteria and are explained by shared fluctuations in the driving field; the measured correlation function scales with mean harmonic flux in agreement with a click-detector response model.
conclusion: Strong harmonic correlations do not by themselves imply nonclassicality, and careful detector modeling is essential when interpreting photon-number correlations in driven nonlinear optical systems.

title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution On Live Quantum States For Ftqc
authors: Yueqi Chen Yicheng Guang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.
tldr: Froq enables safe speculative execution on live quantum states in fault-tolerant quantum computing by using compiler-assisted recovery contracts and resource-aware runtime recovery.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum programs can stall on slow classical error-correction decoders, and existing speculative decoding only accelerates the classical side while quantum operations still wait for confirmed results.
method: The paper proposes compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track misprediction propagation through quantum operations and a runtime mechanism that reserves recovery workspace while balancing speculation benefits against recovery costs.
result: Across eight FTQC programs and 88 configurations, Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% on average, by 18.34% for configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and by up to 31.1% at code distance d=21.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that speculative execution can be extended to quantum-side execution safely, though its contribution is primarily systems/runtime optimization rather than a core quantum information theory result.

title: Coherent Control Of Single-Photon Emission In Broadband Plasmonic Resonators
authors: Athul S. Rema, Adri\'an E. Rubio L\'opez, Felipe Herrera
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic optical nanocavities is challenging due to ultrafast relaxation induced by the broadband nature of the plasmonic near field. Using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics theory, we demonstrate that an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field that is driven by a pulsed laser with frequency comb spectrum undergoes spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses whose amplitude scales quadratically with the number of frequency comb components due to coherent accumulation, and ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles with duration set by the light-matter coupling strength. Conditions are discussed for exponentially suppressing the probability of two or more emission events within the lifetime of the coupled emitter-nanocavity system. The spectral signatures of the optimal one-photon wavepackets are discussed. This work paves the way for the development of ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules in optical nanocavities.
tldr: The paper theoretically demonstrates coherent control of single-photon emission from an emitter strongly coupled to a broadband plasmonic nanocavity driven by a frequency-comb laser.
motivation: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic nanocavities is difficult due to ultrafast plasmonic relaxation, so the authors seek a route to well-resolved one-photon pulses in such broadband plasmonic systems.
method: Using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, they model an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field driven by a pulsed frequency-comb laser and analyze the emission dynamics and photon statistics.
result: They find spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses with amplitudes scaling quadratically with the number of comb components and ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles set by the light-matter coupling strength, with conditions for exponentially suppressing multi-photon emission.
conclusion: The work suggests a path toward ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules in optical nanocavities, with potential relevance to hybrid quantum photonic platforms.

title: Revealing The Hidden Symmetry Of The Asymmetric Quantum Rabi Model
authors: Zi-Min Li, Zi-Cheng Liu, Long-Jie Li, Xuan Zou, Jin-Xiang Fu, Xilin Lu, Murray T. Batchelor
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A longitudinal bias breaks ordinary parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact crossings reappear when the bias equals an integer multiple [MATH] of the oscillator energy spacing. We trace the hidden symmetry to exchange between equal-energy partners [MATH] rungs apart on two displaced oscillator ladders. Tunneling to other rungs makes this exchange vary in time. We construct the exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherences that cancel this variation. At nonzero coupling and tunneling, the resulting charge has no zero modes, and its sign divides the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix. Spin-resolved mirror interference probes coherence between the two opposite-parity states at a crossing. Its small-displacement exponent gives [MATH], and its leading coefficient, together with the charge magnitude, predicts the mixing induced by a slight change in bias.
tldr: The paper identifies a hidden symmetry in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model at integer bias values, constructing an exact generalized-parity operator from spin-oscillator coherences that explains exact spectral crossings and divides the Hilbert space into non-mixing sectors.
motivation: A longitudinal bias breaks ordinary parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact crossings reappear at integer multiples of the oscillator energy spacing, motivating a deeper symmetry explanation.
method: The authors trace the symmetry to exchange between equal-energy rungs on displaced oscillator ladders and construct an exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherence terms that cancel time variation from tunneling.
result: At nonzero coupling and tunneling the resulting charge has no zero modes, and its sign divides the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix; spin-resolved mirror interference probes coherence at a crossing and predicts bias-induced mixing.
conclusion: The work provides an exact hidden-symmetry description of the asymmetric quantum Rabi model and proposes an interference-based signature for observing the associated generalized-parity structure.

title: Excited-state Lifetime And Decay Mechanisms In Erbium-doped Zblan Using Variable Excited-State dual-Pump Analysis
authors: Clement Chan, Thomas J. de Prinse, Jillian E. Moffatt, Nigel A. Spooner, David J. Ottaway, Ori Henderson-Sapir
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a new technique for measuring excited-state lifetimes of rare-earth ions. This technique is particularly powerful for states that are very short lived or have a low photon yield because their de-excitation pathways are dominated by non-radiative processes. The technique uses dual optical parametric oscillators, whose pulses are separated by a variable delay. It reconstructs the excited-state decay curve from a series of delayed fluorescence intensity spectra rather than directly recording the fluorescence decay as done in conventional time-resolved laser fluorescence spectroscopy. The power of the technique is demonstrated by measuring the lifetime of the short-lived [MATH] level in Er[MATH]-doped ZBLAN, which is well-known for its low photon yield. The technique enables accurate measurement of its lifetime and suggests a new depopulating mechanism involving the [MATH] level in ZBLAN glass. Its accuracy is validated by measuring the lifetime of the [MATH] state achieving excellent agreement with conventional time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy measurements. The approach is well suited for measuring lifetimes ranging from the sub-microsecond to the millisecond range. It provides a versatile platform for investigating excited-state dynamics and energy-transfer processes in RE-doped materials.
tldr: A new dual-pump pump-probe technique measures short, low-yield excited-state lifetimes in Er3+-doped ZBLAN glass, applied to the short-lived level relevant to population dynamics.
motivation: Conventional time-resolved laser fluorescence spectroscopy struggles with states that decay mainly non-radiatively or emit few photons, so a method robust to low photon yield is needed to characterize rare-earth level dynamics.
method: Two optical parametric oscillators with a variable inter-pulse delay reconstruct the excited-state decay curve from delayed fluorescence intensity spectra rather than from direct temporal fluorescence decay.
result: The lifetime of the short-lived level in Er3+-doped ZBLAN is measured, a new depopulating mechanism involving that level is proposed, and the method is validated against conventional time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy on a longer-lived reference state.
conclusion: The approach covers sub-microsecond to millisecond lifetimes and offers a versatile platform for excited-state dynamics and energy-transfer studies in rare-earth-doped materials.

title: Nonequilibrium Fluctuations Could Explain The Hot Mitochondria Paradox
authors: Benjamin B. Machta Matthew P. Leighton
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several different experiments have found apparent temperature differences of up to 10 K between the interior of mitochondria and the rest of the cellular environment. The physics of heat conduction, however, precludes the steady-state existence of a temperature difference greater than the microkelvin scale within the cell, absent a far greater energy budget. Nearly a decade after the first reported measurement, this apparent paradox remains unexplained. Here, we propose an explanation which allows the elevated temperature measurements to coexist with the theoretical impossibility of a true 10 K steady-state temperature difference. We suggest that nonequilibrium fluctuations within the cellular environment, combined with molecular temperature probes sensitive to specific ranges of frequencies, can lead to apparent 10 K temperature differences with a biologically attainable power budget.
tldr: The paper proposes that nonequilibrium fluctuations combined with frequency-selective molecular temperature probes can explain apparent 10 K mitochondrial temperature differences without requiring a true steady-state temperature gradient.
motivation: Experiments report large apparent temperature differences inside mitochondria, but heat conduction physics forbids such steady-state gradients at biologically plausible power budgets, creating a longstanding paradox.
method: The authors present a conceptual and quantitative mechanism in which nonequilibrium fluctuations in the cellular environment are interpreted by molecular probes sensitive only to specific frequency ranges.
result: This mechanism can produce apparent 10 K temperature readings while remaining consistent with heat conduction constraints and a biologically attainable energy budget.
conclusion: The mitochondrial hot-temperature paradox may be an artifact of nonequilibrium fluctuation sensing rather than evidence for a true steady-state temperature difference.

title: Verification And Evaluation Of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
authors: Bhuwan Joshi, Zoukarneini Difaizi Tagba, Zhi Xiang Chong, Liyi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to [MATH] by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a [MATH] gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.
tldr: The QBlue verified compiler for Hamiltonian simulation is extended to block-encoding-based algorithms in the Rocq proof assistant and empirically benchmarked against PennyLane on 279 programs.
motivation: Most quantum compilers for Hamiltonian simulation provide no machine-checked guarantee that the output circuits approximate the target evolution, and the earlier QBlue effort covered only Trotter-based methods.
method: Formal verification, in Rocq, of block-encoding-based Hamiltonian simulation algorithms added to the existing end-to-end certified error-bound framework, plus an empirical comparison of 279 programs against PennyLane and between Trotter- and BE-based approaches.
result: The extended compiler yields large gate-count reductions relative to PennyLane on many instances, uncovers bugs in PennyLane, and finds that Trotter-based algorithms can be practically competitive despite the theoretical advantage of block-encoding methods.
conclusion: Certified compilation of Hamiltonian simulation is feasible and practically useful, and the practical Trotter-vs-block-encoding trade-off may differ from the theoretical one.

title: Quisa: A Compact, Flexible And Unified Instruction-Set Coprocessor For Qr-uov Signature
authors: Malik Imran, Ciara Rafferty, Ayesha Khalid, Maire O'neill
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: QR-UOV is a Quotient Ring Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) multivariate quadratic (MQ) signature scheme that has progressed to round-3 of the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) additional signatures call by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Until now, for architectural efficiency and performance trade-offs, QR-UOV has been evaluated only on software platforms and has never been considered on hardware, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). To address this, we are the first to provide a complete QR-UOV hardware implementation through a flexible and unified QUISA coprocessor design, which supports instruction-driven execution for key generation, signing, and verification across all three NIST security levels (SL-I, SL-III, SL-V). The proposed architecture features extensive throughput optimizations by parallelizing key QR-UOV module operations, such as the pseudorandom byte generator, hashing, and rejection sampling. To minimize hardware resources, we propose a modular arithmetic unit with finite-field reduction based on the shift-add folding method. The design introduces a linear system solver for QUISA based on LU decomposition with partial pivoting and a sample solution module, operating over the prime field Fq (q = 127). We comprehensively evaluate QUISA on an Artix-7 FPGA at 80 MHz up to the post-place-and-route stage, utilizing 11,144 slices and 35,248 look-up tables. For higher SL-V security levels, it completes key generation, signing, and verification in 30.4M, 3.8M, and 2.8M clock cycles, respectively.
tldr: QUISA is the first complete FPGA-based instruction-set coprocessor for the QR-UOV post-quantum multivariate signature scheme, supporting key generation, signing and verification across all three NIST security levels.
motivation: QR-UOV has advanced to round 3 of NIST's additional post-quantum signature standardization, yet it has only been evaluated in software; no hardware architecture existed to assess area/performance trade-offs.
method: The authors design a flexible, unified instruction-driven coprocessor with parallelized pseudorandom byte generation, hashing and rejection sampling, a shift-add folding modular arithmetic unit over F_q (q=127), and an LU-decomposition linear system solver with partial pivoting.
result: Implemented on an Artix-7 FPGA at 80 MHz through post-place-and-route, the design uses 11,144 slices and 35,248 LUTs, achieving SL-V key generation, signing and verification in 30.4M, 3.8M and 2.8M clock cycles respectively.
conclusion: The work establishes the first hardware baseline for QR-UOV, showing that a compact unified coprocessor can deliver practical performance across security levels, but it is primarily an applied cryptographic-engineering contribution.

title: Simplified Plotkin-type Bounds For Function-Correcting Codes With b-Symbol And Sum-Rank Distances
authors: Sachin Sampath H., N. T. Rashid Ummer, B. Sundar Rajan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Function-correcting codes (FCCs) are a coding framework that enables reliable communication with minimal redundancy while ensuring the recovery of specific functions of transmitted messages. FCCs have been studied recently under the [MATH]-symbol distance and the sum-rank distance. Existing general Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under these distances require computing the pairwise distances between vectors that map to different function values. As a result, these bounds are often computationally difficult to determine. In this paper, we derive simplified Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under the [MATH]-symbol and sum-rank distances. These bounds depend only on the number of message vectors corresponding to each function value and the sum of pairwise distances among vectors mapped to the same function value. The proposed bounds apply to arbitrary functions and are considerably easier to evaluate than existing Plotkin-type bounds. The known simplified bounds for linear functions under the [MATH]-symbol and sum-rank distances are subsumed as special cases of the proposed bounds. Furthermore, we obtain a tighter bound for linear functions under the sum-rank distance than the existing bound.
tldr: The paper derives simplified Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of function-correcting codes under b-symbol and sum-rank distance metrics.
motivation: Existing general Plotkin-type bounds for function-correcting codes require computing pairwise distances between vectors mapping to different function values, which is computationally prohibitive; simpler, tractable bounds are needed.
method: The authors re-express the bounds so that they depend only on the number of message vectors per function value and the sum of pairwise distances among vectors mapping to the same function value, covering arbitrary functions.
result: The new bounds are considerably easier to evaluate than prior Plotkin-type bounds, subsume known simplified bounds for linear functions as special cases, and yield a tighter bound for linear functions under sum-rank distance.
conclusion: The simplified bounds make redundancy estimates for function-correcting codes practically computable and improve upon existing results in the linear-function case.

title: Learning Free Energy Across A Differentiable Temperature Range By Deep Generative Modeling
authors: Yaowen Zhang, Chen Chen, Wanyu Lin, Shuo-Hui Li, Ding Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Free energy governs the directionality, stability, and temperature sensitivity of physical, chemical, and biological transformations. Conventional free energy calculations, such as thermodynamic integration and free energy perturbation, often have to be performed at individual temperatures and are limited by the high cost of sampling an extensive set of thermodynamic states. Here, we introduce learned temperature-differentiable free energy perturbation (TD-FEP), a deep generative framework that learns a temperature-conditioned, invertible mapping between reference and target systems through data-free, energy-based optimization. TD-FEP thereby unifies one-shot state generation and free energy calculation across a continuous temperature range. We validated TD-FEP across a broad range of applications, including isolated molecules, periodic materials, and chemical reactions.
tldr: TD-FEP is a deep generative framework that learns a temperature-conditioned invertible mapping between reference and target systems, enabling one-shot free energy estimation across a continuous temperature range.
motivation: Conventional free energy methods such as thermodynamic integration and free energy perturbation must be repeated at each temperature and are bottlenecked by the cost of sampling many intermediate thermodynamic states.
method: The authors train an energy-based, data-free generative model that learns an invertible transformation between a reference and target system conditioned on temperature, so that free energy differences and state samples are obtained simultaneously for any temperature in a continuous range.
result: TD-FEP was validated on isolated molecules, periodic materials, and chemical reactions, reproducing free energies across temperatures in a single training run rather than per-temperature simulations.
conclusion: Temperature-differentiable generative modeling offers an efficient route to free energy landscapes in chemistry and materials science, though the work is a classical computational-statistical-mechanics contribution rather than one touching quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: Subquantum Pilot-Wave System Theory: Structural And Amplitude Nonequilibrium Under Source Fields
authors: Said Mikki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.28506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A source in the Schrodinger equation changes the norm of the guiding wave, apparently conflicting with the conservation of probability.
